note:
Corroborating evidence from `/issue 2271` (2026-08-22): two more instances of the
insufficient-bracket failure, in a SECOND false-positive direction worth naming
explicitly in the fix.

#2415's Goal already covers this rule. Recording here instead of filing a
duplicate task (the pre-file sibling check found this one).

## The direction these two add

#2415's title frames the failure as the probe SELF-matching "when the same
command references the unbracketed literal." Both instances below are the
neighbouring shape: the bracketed pattern matched a DIFFERENT LIVE SESSION's
command line, because a `pytest` argv enumerates its test FILES and the module
name appears inside those filenames as a plain substring.

1. `pgrep -af 'pytes[t] .*test_hub'` — intended to find this session's own
   `tests/test_hub.py` run. Matched issue 2273's Step 9c sweep, whose argv lists
   ~180 test files including `tests/test_hub_dir_filecount_guard.py`.

2. `pgrep -af 'workflow_lin[t]\.py'` — intended to find this session's
   `scripts/workflow_lint.py` process. Matched the same foreign pytest argv,
   which lists `tests/test_workflow_lint.py`,
   `tests/test_workflow_lint_agent_spec_caps.py`, and ~15 more
   `test_workflow_lint_*.py` siblings.

In both cases the bracket trick worked as designed — it prevented self-match.
What it cannot do is distinguish "a process running X" from "a process whose
arguments mention X."

## What made them harmless here, and what would not have

Both were caught because the matched argv carried
`--junitxml=/tmp/step9c-junit-issue-2273.xml` — a foreign issue number visible
in the same line. Neither misread changed a decision.

That rescue is luck, not structure. The same probe run against a sibling with no
issue-numbered token in its argv would have read as a live owner of THIS
session's work, and the prescribed consequence of a live-owner read is to DEFER
— so the failure mode is a self-inflicted deadlock (wait forever for a process
that was never yours), not a race. Worth stating in the rule, since "defer to
the live owner" is the safe-looking direction.

## Probe shape that survived

Anchoring to the invocation form rather than the bare module name:

    pgrep -af 'python scripts/workflow_lin[t]\.py *$'

That returned exactly the one real process (pid 3838722) where the unanchored
form returned three, two of them foreign. The general shape is to anchor on the
interpreter-plus-path prefix and, where the invocation takes no arguments, the
end-of-line `*$`.

A complementary discriminator when anchoring is not possible: read the matched
line for an issue-scoped token (`--junitxml=…issue-<M>.xml`, `--basetemp=…`, a
worktree path) and treat a foreign one as proof the match is not yours. That is
what actually saved both probes above.
